  • With a coding agent — the section overview.

docs.title: The dev bridge
docs.text: The dev bridge lets a coding agent see and drive your running app, and check its own change. Set up registers its MCP server with your agent. From then on, every tool call reaches the app you have running.

docs.title: Let it check its own change
docs.text: Ask for a change, in chat or on a mark: "make the counter's button wider". The agent edits the file, your window reloads, and the agent reads the widget tree back and clicks the button before it answers. Your own clicks and keys in the app, the reloads and the app's errors are logs it reads too.

docs.title: Know what it sees of you
docs.text:
• What you type is never recorded. The log of your actions keeps clicks, shortcut keys and scrolls. A burst of typing collapses to one content-free marker.
  • Only your comments reach the agent in your words. It answers on the mark, and you reply there.

docs.title: Know what to expect from it
docs.text:
• A handler that raises leaves the screen unchanged. The agent finds the traceback in the app's error log, and so can you: python -m nuiitivet.dev runtime-log.
  • Its screenshot is not a capture of your window. Your screen can be visibly garbled while its image comes back clean. For a problem you are seeing, send it your own screenshot.
  • The health check flags any single-colour frame as blank, an intentionally solid screen too.
  • Profiling slows frames by roughly 10% while it records. No cost outside a recording.
  • It never runs in production. The bridge lives inside the dev runner. python app.py opens no port.

docs.title: Watch it act on screen
docs.text: The action overlay marks each action the agent takes on your screen. It is on under the dev runner. NUIITIVET_DEV_ACTION_OVERLAY=0 turns it off. Its markers are indigo; comment mode's are amber.

docs.title: Drive the app without an MCP host
docs.text:
The same primitives are one-shot CLI subcommands. They need no [dev] extra:

python -m nuiitivet.dev status
python -m nuiitivet.dev describe-tree
python -m nuiitivet.dev click --label increment

Each subcommand talks to an already-running python -m nuiitivet.dev run <app.py> process over localhost. If none is found, it says so and exits.

docs.title: Address a secondary window
docs.text:
An app with more than one window lists them under status, and the subcommands that reach a window — describe-tree, describe-state, screenshot, click, scroll, scroll-into-view, type, key, wait-for — take --window <id> to pick one:

python -m nuiitivet.dev status                       # {"windows": [{"id": 1, ...}, {"id": 2, ...}]}
python -m nuiitivet.dev describe-tree --window 2
python -m nuiitivet.dev click --key close --window 2

An id no open window answers to fails with that reason rather than quietly falling back to the main window. The MCP tools take the same ids as a window argument.

docs.title: Every marker
docs.text: Action What you see click A pulse at the resolved target, plus its key / label. A raw-coordinate click shows a bare point instead. scroll / scroll_into_view A chevron drifting along the scroll direction as it fades, captioned in words (scroll down feed). type A caret marker near the focused widget. The typed content is never drawn. key The keystroke as a human-readable combo (e.g. Ctrl+Enter), in the corner caption stack.

docs.title: Every command
docs.text:
python -m nuiitivet.dev status
python -m nuiitivet.dev describe-tree
python -m nuiitivet.dev describe-state

docs.title: Hot Reload
docs.text: Edit a widget, save, and see the UI update without a restart.

docs.title: Reload an edit
docs.text: Change "increment" to "add one" in the counter's build() and save. The counter is the one from Set up, running under the dev runner. The button relabels in the open window. The count keeps its value. Saves anywhere under your app's directory reload.

docs.title: If a save fails
docs.text: A syntax or build error on save leaves the previous UI running. The full traceback goes to the console (VS Code debug console / terminal). A banner appears over the app. Fix the code and save again.

docs.title: Reload while debugging in VS Code
docs.text: Hot reload works under the standard F5 debugger with no extension. Breakpoints keep firing in the reloaded code. A save made while stopped at a breakpoint is queued and applied when you resume.

docs.title: If state resets or a screen closes after a save
docs.text: Pattern After the save What to do A keyless widget holding an Observable, when widgets before it are added, removed or reordered The Observable resets to its initial value Give the widget a key An Observable at module top level, or work done in main() The value resets. What main() set up is not redone Create it inside the root factory A widget pushed with Navigator.push(widget) It closes, with every widget pushed above it Push an intent: Navigator.push(intent) A widget shown on the Overlay: Overlay.dialog(widget), Overlay.side_sheet(widget), Overlay.bottom_sheet(widget) It closes Show an intent: Overlay.dialog(intent), Overlay.side_sheet(intent), Overlay.bottom_sheet(intent) await Overlay.dialog(intent) still waiting at the save The dialog stays open, but the result it returns after the save does not appear on screen Close the dialog and open it again after the save

docs.title: Next Steps
docs.text:
• Comment mode — tell the coding agent what to change from the app's own screen.
  • With a coding agent — the section overview.

docs.title: Layout edit mode
docs.text: Some fixes are not worth asking an agent for: a width, or a button outlined instead of filled. Layout edit mode lets you make those yourself, on the app's own screen.

docs.title: 1. Enter the mode
docs.text: Press Ctrl+Shift+E (Cmd+Shift+E on macOS). The mode's name and H help show at the centre for a moment. Inside comment mode the same chord switches over, your marks kept. Ctrl+Shift+C switches back.

docs.title: 2. Select the widget
docs.text: Hover, and the widget under the cursor gets teal corner brackets and a caption naming its type. Hovering a button's label brackets the button. Click to select the widget. The selection stays until you click another widget or click nothing. It keeps its brackets while the pointer is on it, over its children too. Once the pointer leaves, a faint pair of brackets stays. When the container is what you want and its children cover every pixel of it, select a child and press W: W moves the selection to its parent, S back down.

docs.title: 3. Drag a corner
docs.text: Drag a corner bracket. A dashed ghost follows the pointer, captioned with the value that will be written (w 240 | h auto). Esc before the release cancels the drag. The corner is one way to change the widget; its body, its handles and the bar over it are the others, each listed under Everything you can change in place of this step.

docs.title: 4. Release, and read the badge
docs.text: Every drag ends on release. A pick ends on its row. The value is written into the call that built the widget. Hot reload applies it. The ghost stays until the reload lands. When one call builds many widgets, a helper returning a card called from a loop, every one of them gets a ghost, and the caption counts them (14 widgets). After the reload, a notice at the window's bottom-left, the badge, reports anything that did not go as the ghost said: a size that landed elsewhere, or a reload that failed on the edit.

docs.title: 5. Undo if it went wrong
docs.text: Ctrl+Z reverts the last edit this mode wrote. The one exception is a line you have edited by hand since: the undo is refused. Ctrl+Shift+Z redoes what Ctrl+Z undid. A new edit clears what could be redone.

docs.title: 6. Leave
docs.text: Press Esc. With a widget selected, the first press drops the selection and its bar; the second leaves.

docs.title: Everything you can change
docs.text: Each way below takes the place of step 3 of the round. The body's drag depends on its direction: along the container's axis it reorders, across it aligns, into another container it moves.

docs.title: Resize: drag a corner
docs.text:
Drag a corner bracket. A dashed ghost follows the pointer, captioned with the value that will be written (w 240 | h auto), one of the three sizes a widget accepts:

  • "auto" when you release within a few pixels of the widget's natural size;
  • "wt" when you release where a weight would land: at a Column's full width, or at the share of the leftover a weight gets along the main axis; the caption reads wt there;
  • the integer otherwise.

A widget with a size parameter (Icon) stays square: the larger of the two deltas wins.

Hold Alt to land on an exact size: the pointer's pixel count is written instead of a snapped value. W / A / S / D while dragging a corner move it by one pixel. From the first press the mouse no longer moves it. auto / wt are then written only when the corner lands exactly on them.

docs.title: Reorder, or move into another container
docs.text: Drag the body along the container's axis to reorder among its siblings, or into another container to move it there. To drag a container whose children cover it, press in its padding, away from the midpoints of its edges. The container it would land in, its own or another under the pointer, is tinted. An insertion line marks the slot, captioned with the sibling it goes before. A "wt" moves as written. The badge notes when its meaning changed with the move: a "wt" that filled a Column's width becomes a share of a Row's leftover.

docs.title: In a Column, a Row, a Flow or a UniformFlow
docs.text: Up and down reorder in a Column, left and right in a Row. In a Flow or UniformFlow, any travel that leaves the widget's slot reorders.

docs.title: Into or out of a Grid
docs.text: The cell under the pointer is tinted instead of a line. Its caption names the row and column, or the area name, and whoever already sits there. A widget that leaves a Grid leaves its GridItem behind, and the badge names the width / height / padding / alignment the item carried.

docs.title: Over a Stack
docs.text: A list beside the stack names its layers, bottom to top, with the landing marked. A widget dragged in from outside lands in the top layer: inside it when the layer is a container, otherwise on top of the stack. It never lands in the background box underneath. A widget that started inside the stack stays in its own layer wherever the pointer is, so a card under a floating button still reorders in its column. W / S step the landing to another layer, and a digit 0–9 picks one by its number in the list. Past the top layer is a new one on top. The choice holds until the pointer leaves the stack.

docs.title: Into or out of a Container or a Box
docs.text: An empty box takes a widget dropped on it as its child. A box that already has a child is passed over, and the drop lands in the list around it. A widget that leaves a box leaves it behind, empty.

docs.title: Align
docs.text: Drag the body across the container's axis: left and right in a Column, up and down in a Row. In a Flow or UniformFlow, a drag that stays in the widget's slot aligns. In a Flow, it must be mostly up or down; mostly sideways within the slot, it does nothing. In a Stack, a Container or a Box, a drag in any direction aligns. The widget snaps to start / center / end on each axis. A dashed rect marks where every child of the container will land. The caption names the value (center, bottom-right) and how many children move. The alignment written is the container's. A CrossAligned you wrote yourself is respected: dragging its child rewrites that value. Other children with their own CrossAligned stay put when the container's alignment changes.

docs.title: Space it: the handles
docs.text: A hovered widget that takes a padding has an outlined pill, a handle, on each of its four edges. A Column or Row has one more in each gap between its children. Hover a handle and it fills, along with every handle that moves with it.

docs.title: Drag a handle
docs.text:
Pull a padding handle away from the content and the padding grows. The content's edge is zero; pushing past it stays at zero. Push a gap handle toward the next child, down in a Column or right in a Row, and the gap grows. Every gap handle moves together, and every later child is drawn where the new gap puts it. A tinted band shows the value, from the content's edge out to the handle. Its caption is what will be written (padding 20, gap 12). Values snap to multiples of 4. Alt and W / A / S / D work as on a corner.

On an axis the widget sizes to its content, the band grows outward and the handle rides with it. On a fixed width or height, a "wt", or a root that fills its window, the band grows inward from the edge instead: the content moves, and the handle does not follow the pointer.

docs.title: Click a handle
docs.text: Click a handle and the fill turns: every side moves as one (padding=20), then the pair the handle belongs to (padding=(20, 8)), then the one side alone (padding=(8, 8, 20, 8)), and round again. The shape starts as the source spells it.

docs.title: Pick a preset: the bar over the selection
docs.text:
Select a widget whose style has presets, a button of any kind, a card, a chip, a text field or a slider among them, or a Text, and a bar appears just over it. The bar carries the widget's type, then a box for the preset and one for each argument the preset takes: style and size for a button, style alone for a card, type scale for a text. Each box shows what the source holds. Click a box and its list opens under it. Click a row to write it. W / S or ↑ / ↓ move along the list, Enter writes, Esc closes it.

A box reads filled (default) when the call passes no style; a pick inserts the keyword. It reads custom when the value is not a preset, such as a copy_with(...), a variable or a constructor. A pick then replaces that whole expression.

docs.title: Edit the text
docs.text: Enter, or a second click on the selection, edits its text in place. A field opens over the widget. Enter writes the new string into the literal the code passed (text= / label=, or the first argument). Esc or a click elsewhere cancels. The field edits like a text field: Shift+←/→ selects, Ctrl+A/C/X/V (Cmd on macOS) select all, copy, cut and paste. Text that comes from a variable, an f-string or a function call cannot be edited here — the badge says so.

docs.title: Delete
docs.text: Delete / Backspace removes the selected widget from the source — its whole expression, children included. No confirmation. A handler or import the widget used stays behind for you or the agent to clean up.

docs.title: Every gesture
docs.text: Gesture What it does Ctrl+Shift+E Enter layout edit mode (Cmd+Shift+E on macOS). Inside comment mode it switches directly, your marks kept; Ctrl+Shift+C switches back. Hold H Show every gesture of this mode while the key is down. Hover The widget under the cursor gets teal corner brackets, a caption naming its type, and handles on its edges and in its gaps. Click Select it. W / S then move to its parent and back. The selection stays until another click or Esc. Drag a corner bracket Resize. A dashed ghost follows the pointer, captioned with the value that will be written. Drag a handle Change the padding on that side, or the gap. A band shows the value; away from the content is more. Click a handle Turn how many sides move with it: every side, its pair, or itself alone. W / A / S / D while dragging a corner or a handle Move it by one pixel; the mouse no longer moves it. Alt while dragging Land on the exact pixel count instead of snapping. Drag the body Reorder among its siblings, move into the container or grid cell under the pointer, or, keeping its place, align it. W / S / 0–9 while dragging over a Stack Pick the layer the widget lands in; past the top layer is a new one. Release Write and reload. The ghost stays until the reload lands. Click a box on the bar over the selection Open its list of presets; a row writes. W / S move along it, Enter writes, Esc closes. Enter, or a second click on the selection Edit its text in place; Enter writes, Esc or a click elsewhere cancels. Delete / Backspace Remove the selected widget from the source, children included. Ctrl+Z Undo the last edit this mode wrote. Ctrl+Shift+Z Redo what Ctrl+Z undid. A new edit clears what could be redone. Esc Cancel the drag in flight, or close the open list; otherwise drop the selection; with none, leave.

docs.title: Everything it writes, refuses, or ignores
What it writes
docs.text:
Layout edit mode writes these, and nothing else:

  • width, height and size;
  • a child's place in the list that orders the children — children=[...], or the data a comprehension or Column.builder() iterates, even one bound to a name (tags = [...]);
  • a GridItem's row / column or area, with the wrapper itself added or removed as a widget enters or leaves a Grid;
  • a container's alignment / cross_alignment / item_alignment, or a CrossAligned's value;
  • padding and gap, in the shape the handles stand for: one int, an (h, v) pair, or four sides;
  • style as a preset call (nv.ButtonStyle.outlined("m")), and type_scale as a role (nv.TypeScale.TITLE_LARGE); a module that imports Button itself gets ButtonStyle.outlined("m").

It does not write colours, shapes or the other values inside a style.

docs.title: What it refuses
docs.text:
The badge says why, and the file is left alone. That happens for:

  • Resize
  • a size bound to a name or an expression (width=self.card_w);
  • a widget whose constructor takes no width, height or size;
  • Reorder
  • a reorder whose order is not in one list literal in the file — head + tail, [first, *rest], a filtered comprehension, items from a call or a view model, a name that is assigned twice or used again after its list. The badge names the list;
  • a move out of, or into, a container whose children are not written as a list literal — Column.builder(), a ForEach, a comprehension. The badge says so while you hover, before you release;
  • a GridItem whose row / column or area name is bound to a name or an expression; it can neither change cell nor leave the grid;
  • a move into a Grid written as a bare Grid(...) in a module that does not import GridItem: no import is added, and the badge asks you for one;
  • Align
  • an alignment / cross_alignment / item_alignment bound to a name or an expression;
  • a widget as big as its container on every axis it could align on: "wt", or the same size;
  • Space
  • a padding or gap bound to a name, an expression or an observable;
  • Pick
  • a style or type_scale that may come through **kwargs;
  • a bare Button(...) in a module that does not import ButtonStyle (likewise Card / CardStyle, Text / TypeScale): no import is added, and the badge asks you for one;
  • Any
  • a widget whose call has moved or changed since the last reload, or one built by code outside your files.

docs.title: What does nothing
docs.text:
No badge, no change:

  • Reorder
  • releasing the widget in its own slot, or its own grid cell;
  • releasing over a Grid's padding, where there is no cell;
  • Align
  • releasing on the alignment the container already has;
  • Space
  • releasing a handle where it started, which is a click: it turns the shape instead;
  • Pick
  • choosing the row the source already holds.

docs.title: Set up
docs.text: Set up connects your coding agent to your running app. Once per project.

docs.title: 1. Install the dev extra
docs.text:
[dev] carries the dev bridge's MCP server.

uvpip 
uv add nuiitivet
uv add --dev 'nuiitivet[dev]'

pip install 'nuiitivet[dev]'

docs.title: 2. Install the skills
docs.text:
The skills says what each of the three does for you. Install all three, by whichever route fits your agent:

From the packageClaude Code pluginBy hand 
python -m nuiitivet.skills install

That installs them into Claude's directory, .claude/skills/. The other destinations:

# personal (available in every project) — for Claude, ~/.claude/skills/
python -m nuiitivet.skills install --user

# another agent's skills directory — e.g. GitHub Copilot
python -m nuiitivet.skills install --dest .github/skills

Re-run it after upgrading nuiitivet.

/plugin marketplace add yuksblog/nuiitivet
/plugin install nuiitivet

The plugin installs the three skills and registers the MCP server.

The skills live in the Nuiitivet repository under skills/. From a checkout, copy the three directories into your agent's skills directory; the example is Claude's:

cp -r path/to/nuiitivet/skills/nuiitivet-* .claude/skills/

Without a checkout, one at a time:

npx degit yuksblog/nuiitivet/skills/nuiitivet-app .claude/skills/nuiitivet-app

docs.title: 3. Register the MCP server
docs.text:
Add python -m nuiitivet.dev mcp to your MCP host's server list. For Claude Code that is .mcp.json at the project root:

macOS / LinuxWindowsClaude Code plugin 
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "nuiitivet-dev": {
      "command": ".venv/bin/python",
      "args": ["-m", "nuiitivet.dev", "mcp"]
    }
  }
}

{
  "mcpServers": {
    "nuiitivet-dev": {
      "command": ".venv\\\\Scripts\\\\python.exe",
      "args": ["-m", "nuiitivet.dev", "mcp"]
    }
  }
}

Nothing to do: the plugin did it in step 2.

The command is relative to where the host starts the server, the project root for Claude Code. If your host starts elsewhere, give the venv's python as an absolute path.

docs.title: 4. Pass a root factory to the window
docs.text:
import nuiitivet.material as nv

class Counter(nv.ComposableWidget):
    def __init__(self) -> None:
        super().__init__()
        self.count = nv.Observable(0)

    def build(self) -> nv.Widget:
        return nv.Column(
            padding=16,
            children=[
                nv.Text(self.count.map(lambda n: f"Count: {n}")),
                nv.Button("increment", on_click=lambda: self._inc()),
            ],
        )

    def _inc(self) -> None:
        self.count.value += 1

def build_root() -> nv.Widget:
    return Counter()

def main() -> None:
    nv.App(nv.Window(content=build_root)).run()

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

Window takes the factory itself, build_root, not a call to it. With Window(content=build_root()) edits stop applying to that window. The dev runner warns about it. With a lambda, or a function defined inside main(), edits to the classes it builds still apply. Edits to its own body stop applying. No warning is logged.

docs.title: 5. Launch under the dev runner
docs.text:
TerminalVS Code 
python -m nuiitivet.dev run path/to/app.py

A package module launches by name:

python -m nuiitivet.dev run --module yourpkg.app

Arguments for your app go after a -- separator. Everything past it becomes the app's sys.argv:

python -m nuiitivet.dev run app.py -- --png out.png

Add this to .vscode/launch.json and press F5:

{
  "name": "nuiitivet: hot reload",
  "type": "debugpy",
  "request": "launch",
  "module": "nuiitivet.dev",
  "args": ["run", "${workspaceFolder}/app.py"],
  "console": "integratedTerminal"
}

Arguments for your app go into args, after a "--" entry.

python app.py still runs the app as before.

docs.title: 6. Confirm the connection
docs.text: Run python -m nuiitivet.dev status, or ask the agent to call status. It prints the running app's window title. Check it is your app. A "no running app" error means the app is not up under the dev runner.

docs.text:

  • With a coding agent — the section overview.

docs.title: The skills
docs.text: A skill is a bundle of instructions your coding agent loads on its own when the task calls for it. The features of this section work without them; the skills are what make the agent use them well. All three are installed in Set up.

docs.title: Have it write idiomatic Nuiitivet
docs.text: nuiitivet-app keeps the agent from writing Nuiitivet with other frameworks' habits. The API resembles Flutter, SwiftUI / Compose and Rx, so left alone the agent writes valid Python with setState, Padding / SizedBox wrappers, and subscribe() to push a value into a widget. The skill carries the idioms and a linter for the habits.

docs.title: Have it run and check the app itself
docs.text: nuiitivet-debug has the agent run your app under hot reload, read the running tree, drive it, and check its own change before it answers — instead of guessing from a screenshot or racing a spinner.

docs.title: Have it read your comments and wait for each Send
docs.text: nuiitivet-see-comments has the agent read the comments you wrote on the app and answer on each mark. In chat, /nuiitivet-see-comments watch once per session makes it wait for each Send, handle every comment in a turn, and wait again. Without watch, it reads them once.

docs.title: Source jump
docs.text: Ctrl+Shift+Click (Cmd+Shift+Click on macOS) on a widget opens the code that built it, in your editor.

docs.title: Open a widget's code
docs.text: Hold Ctrl+Shift. The widget under the cursor gets rose brackets and a caption naming its file and line. Click, and the editor opens at that line. A caption then says what happened: opening app.py:42, or why nothing did. It clears on the next pointer move.

docs.title: Use another editor
docs.text:
VS Code works as installed. When the caption says VS Code was not found, a portable install or a fork that answers to vscode://, pass --editor vscode and the jump opens it anyway. For another editor, pass its URL scheme to --editor. {file} and {line} are replaced with the path and the line:

# Cursor
python -m nuiitivet.dev run app.py --editor "cursor://file{file}:{line}:1"
# PyCharm
python -m nuiitivet.dev run app.py \
  --editor "jetbrains://pycharm/navigate/reference?project=NAME&path={file}:{line}"

A template without {file}, {line} or a scheme is refused when the app starts, with the reason.

docs.title: Jump from inside a mode
docs.text: Ctrl+Shift+Click works inside comment mode and layout edit mode too. There it opens the code instead of marking or selecting. Inside comment mode, rose brackets mean a jump; amber means a mark.

docs.title: UI Design System
docs.text: A UI Design System in Nuiitivet defines the look, behavior, and structure of an application as a consistent whole. Nuiitivet currently provides Material Design 3 Expressive as its built-in implementation.

docs.title: Components
docs.text:
Every UI Design System consists of five components:

Component Role App Application entry point and lifecycle manager Overlay Layer management: blocking, pass-through, backdrop Navigator Navigation and routing management Theme Visual configuration Widgets Design-specific implementations of UI elements (buttons, textfields, checkboxes, etc.)

docs.title: Material Design 3 Expressive
docs.text:
import nuiitivet.material as nv
  • Material App
  • Material Overlay
  • Material Navigator
  • Material Theme
  • Material Widgets

docs.title: Font Configuration
docs.text: nuiitivet uses system-installed fonts by default. This guide covers how to load custom font files and reference them by family name throughout your application. All font configuration lives on the nv.Fonts namespace.

docs.title: System fonts
docs.text:
Fonts.set_default_family() sets the global fallback used when no font_family is specified:

import nuiitivet.material as nv

# macOS
nv.Fonts.set_default_family("Hiragino Sans")
# Windows
# nv.Fonts.set_default_family("Yu Gothic")

Pass None to reset to locale-based automatic detection.

docs.title: Bundled fonts with Fonts.register()
docs.text:
When distributing an application with bundled .ttf / .otf files, use Fonts.register() to make them available by name.

import nuiitivet.material as nv

# Call once at startup, before any UI is created.
nv.Fonts.register("assets/fonts/NotoSansJP.ttf", family_name="NotoSansJP")

After registration the family name can be used anywhere a font_family is accepted:

import nuiitivet.material as nv

# Text widget
nv.Text("Hello", style=nv.TextStyle(font_family="NotoSansJP"))

# Icon widget with a custom icon font
nv.Fonts.register("assets/fonts/MyIcons.ttf", family_name="MyIcons")
nv.Icon("star", style=nv.IconStyle(custom_font_family="MyIcons"))

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• Fonts.register() only stores the mapping; the font file is loaded lazily on first use and cached for the lifetime of the process.
  • Call Fonts.register() before any widget is rendered. Calling it after rendering has started may produce stale cache results because resolved typefaces are cached per family name.
  • Relative paths are resolved relative to the working directory at call time. Use pathlib.Path(__file__).parent / "..." for paths relative to your source files.
from pathlib import Path
import nuiitivet.material as nv

_ASSETS = Path(__file__).parent / "assets" / "fonts"
nv.Fonts.register(str(_ASSETS / "NotoSansJP.ttf"), family_name="NotoSansJP")

docs.title: Material App
docs.text: nv.App(nv.Window(content=...)) is the entry point for a Material Design application: the Window sets up the Material Overlay and Navigator, and the App supplies the Material Theme — all with sensible defaults so you can focus on building your UI.

docs.title: Basic Usage
docs.text:
import nuiitivet.material as nv


class HomeScreen(nv.ComposableWidget):
    def build(self) -> nv.Widget:
        return nv.Container(
            alignment="center",
            width="wt",
            height="wt",
            child=nv.Column(
                gap=16,
                children=[
                    nv.Text("Hello, Material Design!"),
                    nv.Button("Get Started", style=nv.ButtonStyle.filled()),
                ],
            ),
        )


nv.App(nv.Window(content=HomeScreen, title="Material App")).run()

docs.title: Window
docs.text:
Control the window size, position, and resize behavior:

import nuiitivet.material as nv

nv.App(
    nv.Window(
        content=HomeScreen,
        width=1280,
        height=800,
        window_position="center",
        resizable=False,
    ),
).run()

See Window for detailed usage.

docs.title: Window Chrome
docs.text:
By default Window uses OS-managed chrome (OSChrome), which draws the standard OS title bar. Set its text with the title= parameter:

import nuiitivet.material as nv

nv.App(nv.Window(content=HomeScreen, title="My App")).run()

docs.title: Custom Chrome
docs.text:
Replace the OS title bar with your own header widget via chrome=CustomChrome(...). Nuiitivet wraps the header in a drag area so the window can still be moved by dragging it:

import nuiitivet.material as nv

header = nv.Row(
    children=[nv.Text("My App")],
    cross_alignment="center",
    width="wt",
    height=40,
    padding=(12, 0),
).modifier(nv.background("#1a237e"))

nv.App(
    nv.Window(
        content=HomeScreen,
        title="My App",
        chrome=nv.CustomChrome(header=header, corner_radius=8),
    ),
).run()

See Window Chrome for detailed usage.

docs.title: Theme
docs.text:
Pass a ThemeFactory to change the seed color or switch to dark mode:

import nuiitivet.material as nv

nv.App(nv.Window(content=HomeScreen), theme=nv.ThemeFactory.dark("#00639B")).run()

See Material Theme for detailed usage.

docs.title: Overlay Intents
docs.text:
Register custom overlay intents on the window's overlay. They can be dispatched from anywhere in the widget tree:

import nuiitivet.material as nv


def build_overlay() -> nv.Overlay:
    return nv.Overlay(
        intents={
            MyIntent: lambda intent: nv.BasicDialog(title=intent.title, message=intent.message),
        },
    )


nv.App(nv.Window(content=HomeScreen, overlay=build_overlay)).run()

See Material Overlay for detailed usage.

API Reference

docs.title: Material Navigator
docs.text:
MaterialNavigator is a Material Design 3-flavored subclass of Navigator. It is automatically configured by App.

The only difference from the base Navigator is the default transition: a screen pushed without transition= moves with the MD3 page transition. push(screen, transition=...) overrides it for that screen.

Import convention

App and Navigator are the public names exported from nuiitivet.material for these classes. Import and use them by these names throughout your code.

import nuiitivet.material as nv

The rest of this guide follows this convention.

docs.title: Automatic Setup
docs.text:
Passing a plain Widget to App is all that is needed. App wraps it in a MaterialNavigator automatically.

import nuiitivet.material as nv

nv.App(nv.Window(content=HomeScreen)).run()

docs.title: Accessing
docs.text:
App registers the MaterialNavigator as the root navigator.

import nuiitivet.material as nv

nv.Navigator.of(self)    # root navigator
nv.Navigator.of(self)  # nearest ancestor Navigator — use only with nested navigators

Neither can be resolved from a widget's __init__. Resolve one in the event handler, every time.

docs.title: Further Reading
docs.text:
Topic Guide push / pop basics Navigation Overview Custom transitions Navigation Overview Intent-based routing Intent-Based Navigation Nested navigation Nested Navigation

API Reference

docs.title: Material Overlay
docs.text:
MaterialOverlay is a Material Design 3-flavored subclass of Overlay — the framework's system for displaying content above the main widget tree. It is automatically configured by App.

Import convention

Import App and Overlay from nuiitivet.material.

import nuiitivet.material as nv

The rest of this guide follows this convention.

The base Overlay exposes one primitive, show() — see Primitives for details. MaterialOverlay wraps it with two additions:

  1. Shortcut methods — dialog(), snackbar(), bottom_sheet(), side_sheet(), loading() — each pre-configured with the correct MD3 position and transition.
  2. Intent resolution — shortcuts accept plain data objects (intents) in addition to widgets, decoupling business logic from the widget layer.

docs.title: Accessing Overlay
docs.text:
App owns an Overlay. Reach it from any mounted widget with Overlay.of(self).

import nuiitivet.material as nv

overlay = nv.Overlay.of(self)

The nearest ancestor Overlay wins, falling back to the App's when there is no nested one above you. Pass root=True to skip a nested overlay and target the App's:

overlay = nv.Overlay.of(self, root=True)

Under a MaterialApp the App's overlay is a MaterialOverlay, so MaterialOverlay.of(self) returns it with the subclass type intact and the shortcuts below available. See Overlay for the full lookup rules.

docs.title: Shortcuts at a Glance
docs.text:
Shortcut show() call Scrim dialog() show(dialog, backdrop=True, dismiss_on_outside_tap=...) Fade snackbar() show(widget, passthrough=True, timeout=...) None side_sheet() show(sheet, backdrop=True, dismiss_on_outside_tap=...) Fade bottom_sheet() show(sheet, backdrop=True, dismiss_on_outside_tap=...) Fade loading() show(widget, passthrough=True) None

Every shortcut returns an OverlayHandle. You can await it to receive the result after the overlay closes:

handle = overlay.dialog(...)
result = await handle   # OverlayResult[T]
if result.value is True:
    ...

For a full treatment of the handle/await pattern and MVVM architecture, see Dialogs.

docs.title: Dialog
docs.text:
Displays a modal dialog with a scrim. This is the most common use case; refer to Dialogs for the complete guide including custom dialogs, OverlayAware, and MVVM patterns.

import nuiitivet.material as nv

overlay.dialog(
    nv.BasicDialog(
        title="Delete item?",
        message="This action cannot be undone.",
        actions=[
            nv.Button("Cancel", on_click=lambda: nv.Overlay.of(self).close(None), style=nv.ButtonStyle.text()),
            nv.Button("Delete", on_click=lambda: nv.Overlay.of(self).close(True), style=nv.ButtonStyle.text()),
        ],
    )
)
Parameter Type Default Description dialog Widget \| Any required Dialog widget, or an intent resolved by the overlay dismiss_on_outside_tap bool True Dismiss when tapping the scrim

For a non-standard transition or backdrop, call show() directly. Dialogs do not auto-dismiss, so there is no timeout parameter.

docs.title: Snackbar
docs.text:
Displays a brief, non-blocking message at the bottom of the screen. Background interaction remains active. Automatically dismisses after duration seconds.

overlay.snackbar("Item deleted")

Pass a Snackbar widget for more control over appearance:

import nuiitivet.material as nv

overlay.snackbar(nv.Snackbar("Upload complete"))
Parameter Type Default Description message str \| Snackbar required Message text or a Snackbar widget duration float 3.0 Display duration in seconds

docs.title: Side Sheet
docs.text:
Displays a modal sheet that slides in from a side edge. The slide-in edge is a placement concern owned by side_sheet(): the side argument drives three things at once — the slide direction of the transition, the screen-edge alignment, and which (inner, away-from-edge) corners are rounded. The corner rounding is applied by side_sheet() via the corner_radius modifier, so the SideSheet widget itself renders a square container.

import nuiitivet.material as nv

overlay.side_sheet(
    nv.SideSheet(
        headline="Settings",
        content=nv.Text("Sheet content here"),
    ),
    side="right",
)
Parameter Type Default Description sheet SideSheet \| Any required Side sheet widget, or an intent resolved by the overlay side "right" \| "left" "right" Edge the sheet slides in from dismiss_on_outside_tap bool True Dismiss when tapping the scrim

docs.title: Bottom Sheet
docs.text:
Displays a modal sheet that slides up from the bottom edge. The same principle as side_sheet() applies: the transition direction (slide from bottom), screen-edge position (bottom-center), and corner radii (top two corners rounded, bottom edge flush) must all stay consistent. Because all three are determined solely by the fact that it is a bottom sheet, bottom_sheet() accepts only a BottomSheet widget, or an intent that resolves to one.

import nuiitivet.material as nv

overlay.bottom_sheet(
    nv.BottomSheet(
        headline="Options",
        content=nv.Text("Sheet content here"),
    )
)
Parameter Type Default Description sheet BottomSheet \| Any required Bottom sheet widget, or an intent resolved by the overlay dismiss_on_outside_tap bool True Dismiss when tapping the scrim

docs.title: Loading Indicator
docs.text: Displays a centered loading indicator. The overlay is pass-through — background content remains visible and interactive, and there is no dismiss gesture. Use handle.close(None) or while_loading() to dismiss it.

docs.title: Manual Control
docs.text:
handle = overlay.loading()
perform_long_task()
handle.close(None)

docs.title: Context Manager
docs.text:
while_loading() shows the indicator and guarantees it is dismissed when the block exits, even on exceptions:

async with nv.Overlay.of(self).while_loading():
    await fetch_data()

docs.title: Custom Indicator
docs.text:
async with nv.Overlay.of(self).while_loading(my_custom_widget):
    await fetch_data()

docs.title: Material Design 3 Transitions
docs.text:
Each shortcut applies a pre-configured MD3 transition automatically. All transitions use Material Expressive spring-based easing (EXPRESSIVE_DEFAULT_EFFECTS).

Shortcut Enter Exit Scrim dialog Fade in + scale up from 92% Fade out + scale down to 96% Fades with content snackbar Fade in + slide up 20 px Fade out None bottom_sheet Slide in from bottom edge Slide out to bottom edge Fades with content side_sheet Slide in from side edge Slide out to side edge Fades with content loading Instant Instant None

These shortcuts accept only their typed arguments — a Widget or an intent for dialog(), loading(), bottom_sheet() and side_sheet(), and str/Snackbar for snackbar(). None of them takes a transition or a position: each shortcut owns the MD3 transition, screen-edge position, and (for sheets) corner radii, so they stay consistent. bottom_sheet() derives everything from the fact that it is a bottom sheet; side_sheet() derives it from its side argument.

To display fully custom overlay content with a non-standard transition or backdrop, call show() directly.

docs.title: Intent System
docs.text: Intents let view models request overlays without importing widget classes. Pass a plain data object to a shortcut; Overlay resolves it to the correct widget through its intents.

docs.title: Built-in Intents
docs.text:
Intent Resolves to Shortcut BasicDialogIntent BasicDialog with an OK button dialog() LoadingIntent Built-in LoadingIndicator loading() 
import nuiitivet.material as nv

overlay.dialog(nv.BasicDialogIntent(title="Error", message="Something went wrong."))

docs.title: Custom Intents
docs.text:
Pass a mapping from intent type to widget factory as the overlay's intents, and the overlay factory to the Window:

from dataclasses import dataclass
import nuiitivet.material as nv


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class ConfirmIntent:
    message: str


def build_overlay() -> nv.Overlay:
    return nv.Overlay(
        intents={
            ConfirmIntent: lambda intent: nv.BasicDialog(
                title="Confirm",
                message=intent.message,
                actions=[
                    nv.Button("Cancel", on_click=lambda: nv.Overlay.of(self).close(False), style=nv.ButtonStyle.text()),
                    nv.Button("OK", on_click=lambda: nv.Overlay.of(self).close(True), style=nv.ButtonStyle.text()),
                ],
            ),
        },
    )


nv.App(nv.Window(content=HomeScreen, overlay=build_overlay)).run()

Dispatch from anywhere in the widget tree:

async def on_submit(self) -> None:
    handle = nv.Overlay.of(self).dialog(ConfirmIntent(message="Submit form?"))
    result = await handle
    if result.value is True:
        self.submit()

A sheet shortcut takes an intent the same way. The factory returns the sheet widget, and the shortcut keeps its placement arguments:

from dataclasses import dataclass
import nuiitivet.material as nv


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class SettingsIntent:
    title: str


def build_settings_sheet(intent: SettingsIntent) -> nv.Widget:
    return nv.SideSheet(
        nv.Box(
            nv.Column(
                children=[nv.Text("Setting 1"), nv.Text("Setting 2")],
                gap=12,
                cross_alignment="start",
            ),
            padding=24,
        ),
        headline=intent.title,
    )


def build_overlay() -> nv.Overlay:
    return nv.Overlay(intents={SettingsIntent: build_settings_sheet})


class SheetIntentDemo(nv.ComposableWidget):
    def open_settings(self) -> None:
        nv.Overlay.of(self).side_sheet(SettingsIntent(title="Settings"), side="left")

For more on intents in the context of MVVM architecture, see Dialogs — Architecting Dialogs in MVVM.

API Reference

docs.title: Material Theme
docs.text:
MaterialThemeFactory is a factory that creates Theme objects pre-configured with Material Design 3 color roles derived from a seed color.

Import convention

App and ThemeFactory are the public names exported from nuiitivet.material for these classes. Import and use them by these names throughout your code.

import nuiitivet.material as nv

The rest of this guide follows this convention.

docs.title: Setting the Theme
docs.text: Pass a Theme to App via the theme parameter to apply it to the entire application.

docs.title: No theme
docs.text:
When theme is omitted, App applies the default M3 light theme (#6750A4).

import nuiitivet.material as nv

nv.App(nv.Window(content=HomeScreen)).run()

docs.title: Seed color
docs.text:
Pass a different seed color to generate a distinct M3 palette:

import nuiitivet.material as nv

nv.App(nv.Window(content=HomeScreen), theme=nv.ThemeFactory.light("#00639B")).run()

docs.title: Dark mode
docs.text: nv.App(nv.Window(content=HomeScreen), theme=nv.ThemeFactory.dark("#00639B")).run()

docs.title: Tuning the Palette
docs.text: A seed color does not fully determine the palette. Two further inputs shape how roles are derived from it, and both default to the Material 3 defaults.

docs.title: Scheme variant
docs.text:
variant selects the algorithm that derives the tonal palettes from the seed. It defaults to SchemeVariant.TONAL_SPOT, the M3 default, which keeps colors close to the seed's hue at a moderate chroma.

import nuiitivet.material as nv

nv.App(nv.Window(content=HomeScreen), theme=nv.ThemeFactory.light("#6750A4", variant=nv.SchemeVariant.VIBRANT)).run()
Variant Character TONAL_SPOT M3 default; moderate chroma near the seed hue NEUTRAL Near-grayscale, seed hue barely present MONOCHROME Pure grayscale VIBRANT Maximum chroma; strongly saturated EXPRESSIVE Shifts hue away from the seed for contrast FIDELITY / CONTENT Stays as close to the literal seed color as possible RAINBOW / FRUIT_SALAD Playful multi-hue schemes

docs.title: Contrast level
docs.text:
contrast_level accepts a value in [-1.0, 1.0] and defaults to 0.0. Higher values push foreground roles further from their backgrounds, which helps meet accessibility requirements.

nv.App(nv.Window(content=HomeScreen), theme=nv.ThemeFactory.light("#6750A4", contrast_level=0.5)).run()

Both options are accepted by ThemeFactory.light, dark, from_seed, and from_seed_pair.

docs.title: Choosing the Component Sizes
docs.text:
import nuiitivet.material as nv

nv.App(
    nv.Window(content=build_root),
    # use this: "desktop" (default), "mobile" or a FormFactor
    theme=nv.ThemeFactory.light("#6750A4", form_factor="mobile"),
).run()

form_factor sets how large the controls are. Colors, shapes and font sizes stay the same.

Form factor Sizes "desktop" The default. The controls of one row are 40dp tall: TextField, SearchBar, Button, Checkbox, RadioButton, Switch. A menu item is 32dp. "mobile" The Material Design 3 sizes, built for touch. A TextField is 56dp, and a control smaller than 48dp reserves a 48dp touch target.

See the full runnable demo: samples/design-system/material_theme/form_factor.py

docs.title: If a filled text field loses its label
docs.text:
Under "desktop" a filled TextField shows its label only while the field is empty. A 40dp filled field has no room for a label above the text.

Use TextFieldStyle.outlined() to keep the label on the outline, or put a Text beside the field.

docs.title: Resizing one component in the whole app
docs.text:
Start from a built-in form factor and change one density step. A step takes 4dp off the Material Design 3 height: 0 is 56dp for a TextField, -2 is 48dp.

theme = nv.ThemeFactory.light(
    "#6750A4",
    form_factor=nv.FormFactor.desktop().copy_with(text_field=-2),
)

docs.title: Resizing one widget
docs.text:
A style's density wins over the form factor.

nv.TextField(label="Name", style=nv.TextFieldStyle.outlined().copy_with(density=-2))

docs.title: Switching Themes at Runtime
docs.text: To switch the active theme, call App.of(self).set_theme(...) with a Theme instance or a registered name.

docs.title: Light / Dark Toggle
docs.text:
from_seed_pair generates both a light and a dark Theme from a single seed color. Use an Observable[str] for the button label so it updates reactively without a full rebuild:

import nuiitivet.material as nv

light, dark = nv.ThemeFactory.from_seed_pair("#6750A4")

class HomeScreen(nv.ComposableWidget):
    _is_dark = False

    def on_toggle() -> None:
        next_theme = light if self._is_dark else dark
        nv.App.of(self).set_theme(next_theme)

nv.App(nv.Window(content=HomeScreen), theme=light).run()

See the full runnable demo: samples/design-system/material_theme/light_dark_toggle.py

docs.title: Multiple Themes
docs.text:
When themes are too many to hold in local scope everywhere, register them by name with app.register_themes(...) and switch by string key:

import nuiitivet.material as nv

ocean_light, ocean_dark   = nv.ThemeFactory.from_seed_pair("#00639B")
forest_light, forest_dark = nv.ThemeFactory.from_seed_pair("#386A20")

app = nv.App(nv.Window(content=HomeScreen), theme=ocean_light)

# Register before run() — safe before the event loop starts
app.register_themes({
    "ocean-light":  ocean_light,
    "ocean-dark":   ocean_dark,
    "forest-light": forest_light,
    "forest-dark":  forest_dark,
})

app.run()


# Switch from anywhere in the widget tree
nv.App.of(self).set_theme("forest-dark")

See the full runnable demo: samples/design-system/material_theme/multiple_themes.py

Registry keys and from_seed_pair names

from_seed_pair accepts an optional name argument, but it assigns the same label to both the light and dark Theme — no -light / -dark suffix is appended automatically. The dictionary keys passed to register_themes are the actual lookup keys; choose them freely.

light, dark = nv.ThemeFactory.from_seed_pair("#6750A4", name="brand")
light.name  # "brand"
dark.name   # "brand"  ← same, not "brand-dark"

\"light\" and \"dark\" as built-in fallbacks

set_theme("light") and set_theme("dark") are reserved shortcuts. When no theme with that exact name is registered, they fall back to a plain (non-Material) default theme.

These strings happen to equal the values of Theme.mode, but they are separate concepts — one is a registry lookup key, the other is a property of the Theme object itself.

docs.title: Advanced: Color Roles in Custom Widgets
docs.text:
Target audience

This section is for authors building custom widgets. Built-in Material widgets apply color roles automatically; if you are only composing them, you do not need this.

docs.title: Reading the current theme
docs.text:
Inside any mounted widget, Theme.of(self) returns the active Theme:

import nuiitivet.material as nv

theme = nv.Theme.of(self)
is_dark = theme.mode == "dark"

A theme read in __init__ or on_mount leaves the widget stuck

Read the theme in build(). A widget with no build() reads it in paint().

A widget that reads in __init__ and keeps the value paints light for good, in a dark app too. A widget that reads in on_mount keeps the theme it mounted under and ignores every later set_theme. Neither case raises or logs.

docs.title: Applying a color role
docs.text:
Call theme.extension(MaterialThemeData) to retrieve M3-specific data, then look up a ColorRole:

import nuiitivet.material as nv
from nuiitivet.material.theme.theme_data import MaterialThemeData

mat = nv.Theme.of(self).extension(MaterialThemeData)
if mat is not None:
    surface_color = mat.roles.get(nv.ColorRole.SURFACE_CONTAINER)

ColorRole also provides a resolve shorthand that combines both steps:

color = nv.ColorRole.SURFACE_CONTAINER.resolve(nv.Theme.of(self))  # str | None

Both extension() and resolve() return None outside an initialized widget tree (e.g. during construction), so always guard against None.

docs.title: Example: theme-aware custom widget
docs.text:
import nuiitivet.material as nv


class ThemedCard(nv.ComposableWidget):
    def __init__(self, child: nv.Widget) -> None:
        super().__init__()
        self.child = child

    def build(self) -> nv.Widget:
        bg = nv.ColorRole.SURFACE_CONTAINER.resolve(nv.Theme.of(self)) or "#FFFFFF"
        return nv.Container(color=bg, padding=16, child=self.child)

docs.title: Available Color Roles
docs.text:
Group Roles Primary PRIMARY, ON_PRIMARY, PRIMARY_CONTAINER, ON_PRIMARY_CONTAINER, INVERSE_PRIMARY Secondary SECONDARY, ON_SECONDARY, SECONDARY_CONTAINER, ON_SECONDARY_CONTAINER Tertiary TERTIARY, ON_TERTIARY, TERTIARY_CONTAINER, ON_TERTIARY_CONTAINER Background BACKGROUND, ON_BACKGROUND Surface SURFACE, ON_SURFACE, INVERSE_SURFACE, INVERSE_ON_SURFACE, SURFACE_VARIANT, ON_SURFACE_VARIANT Surface containers SURFACE_CONTAINER_LOWEST, SURFACE_CONTAINER_LOW, SURFACE_CONTAINER, SURFACE_CONTAINER_HIGH, SURFACE_CONTAINER_HIGHEST Outline OUTLINE, OUTLINE_VARIANT Utility SHADOW, SCRIM Error ERROR, ON_ERROR, ERROR_CONTAINER, ON_ERROR_CONTAINER

API Reference

docs.title: Material Widgets
docs.text:
nuiitivet.material implements Material Design 3 widgets, with more on the way. This page showcases the available widgets — each with a screenshot and a link to the API reference. Overlay-based widgets (Dialog, BottomSheet, SideSheet, Loading) are covered in Material Overlay.

Import convention

All widgets shown below are exported from nuiitivet.material:

import nuiitivet.material as nv

docs.title: Text
docs.text:
Typography component for rendering text with theme-aware styles.

API Reference

docs.title: Icon
docs.text:
Material Symbols icon component. Specify a symbol name and an optional size.

API Reference

docs.title: Button
docs.text:
Five M3 button styles — Filled, Tonal, Elevated, Outlined, and Text — plus icon support and disabled state.

API Reference

docs.title: ToggleButton
docs.text:
Two-state button with selected / unselected appearance. Available in Filled and Outlined styles.

API Reference

docs.title: IconButton
docs.text:
Compact icon-only buttons in the standard M3 styles, plus a toggle variant.

API Reference

docs.title: Fab (Floating Action Button)
docs.text:
Prominent action button. Multiple color variants and three sizes (small / medium / large).

API Reference

docs.title: ExtendedFab
docs.text:
FAB with a label beside the icon. Toggle its expanded observable to morph between the extended pill and a circular FAB. Available in tonal and solid color variants across all three sizes.

API Reference

docs.title: FabMenu
docs.text:
M3 Expressive FAB menu. A single is_open observable morphs the FAB between its add and close icons and reveals a stack of labelled FabMenuItem actions, dismissed by tapping outside or selecting an action.

API References: FabMenu ・ FabMenuItem

docs.title: SplitButton
docs.text:
M3 Expressive split button — a leading action button joined to a trailing button that opens a menu. Available in Filled, Tonal, Elevated, and Outlined styles across sizes XS–L.

API Reference

docs.title: ButtonGroup
docs.text:
Group related actions. StandardButtonGroup keeps spacing between buttons; ConnectedButtonGroup connects them as a single segmented control.

API Reference

docs.title: Selection Controls
docs.text:
Checkbox, RadioButton (typically grouped via RadioGroup), and Switch for boolean / single-select input.

API References: Checkbox ・ RadioButton ・ Switch

docs.title: Slider
docs.text:
Numeric input, split by axis. HorizontalSlider / VerticalSlider select a value in a range, the *CenteredSlider variants are anchored at zero, and the *RangeSlider variants select a min/max pair. Horizontal variants are sized with width; vertical variants with height.

API References: HorizontalSlider ・ VerticalSlider ・ HorizontalCenteredSlider ・ VerticalCenteredSlider ・ HorizontalRangeSlider ・ VerticalRangeSlider

docs.title: TextField
docs.text:
Text input, with leading icons, supporting text and error states. The filled and outlined variants come from style; TextField.multiline is the text area.

An Observable passed as value is the field's value — it is displayed, and what the user types is written into it. A read-only source (.map(...), a computed value) has nowhere to write, so it only displays; pair it with disabled=True.

nv.TextField(value=self.query, label="Search")
nv.TextField(value=self.pin, input_filter=nv.digits_only() | nv.max_length(4))
nv.TextField.multiline(value=self.notes, label="Notes", max_lines=4)

Derive what the text means from the observable; on_change is for a side effect only. on_submit fires on every Enter and never on focus loss, and setting it takes Enter from the screen's shortcuts (Interaction modifiers); work for when the user leaves the field goes in on_focus_change. In a multi-line field Shift+Enter breaks the line and Enter still submits. Restricting what can be typed, and finishing a half-typed value on the way out, are recipes in Typed Values from Text Input.

API Reference

docs.title: SearchBar
docs.text:
A search input. DockedSearchBar is the same bar with a panel anchored below it.

value binds exactly as TextField's does — pass an Observable and what the user types is written into it.

nv.SearchBar(self.query, placeholder="Search fruit", width=440)

DockedSearchBar puts one widget in that panel, as content. It holds whatever the query currently calls for — recent searches, suggestions, results, a spinner, "no matches" — and you swap what is inside it from your own observables:

nv.DockedSearchBar(
    self.query,
    placeholder="Search fruit",
    content=nv.Column(
        children=[nv.ForEach(self.matches, lambda item, index: nv.Text(item))],
    ),
    on_submit=self.search,
    width=440,
)

content stays live while the panel is closed, so whatever drives it keeps running. Gate that with your own observable if it is expensive.

docs.title: Opening and closing the panel
docs.text:
The widget drives one observable from these triggers:

Trigger Effect The bar takes focus Open — including on an empty query, where MD3 shows recent searches A tap on the bar Open — so a click brings a closed panel back even while the bar keeps focus The user edits the text Open, even if it was just closed Enter Close, unless you pass close_on_enter=False Escape Close, leaving the bar focused — typing reopens it. With the panel closed, Escape is left for an enclosing handler Focus leaves, or a tap outside Close. The bar itself is not outside: clicking into the text moves the caret and the panel stays up

That default gives you the usual desktop loop for free: Enter puts the panel away, on_submit renders results on the page, and typing again brings the panel back. The close runs before on_submit, so a search that wants the panel to stay up can reopen it from inside its own callback. To keep the results in the panel instead, pass close_on_enter=False and swap content when the search returns.

Only user edits reopen it. Assigning to the bound observable does not, so filling the bar in after the user picks something leaves the panel closed:

def pick(self, item: str) -> None:
    self.query.value = item      # the panel stays closed
    self.search(item)

Pass is_open=self.panel_open to drive the panel from your own Observable[bool], or to react to it opening and closing. Writing to it opens and closes the panel directly; omit it and the widget keeps its own, readable as bar.is_open.

In a window too short for the panel, it keeps its minimum height and extends past the bottom edge rather than covering the bar.

There is no full-screen search widget. Lay the screen out yourself and put a SearchBar in it; the bar keeps its focus animation there.

Not supported: an avatar slot, multiple trailing actions, and a disabled state. trailing_icon is a single generic slot — clearing the query is one thing you can wire it to, not built-in behaviour.

API Reference

docs.title: Card
docs.text:
Container for grouped content. Three variants — Filled, Outlined, Elevated.

API Reference

docs.title: Chip
docs.text:
Compact actions and choices: AssistChip, FilterChip, InputChip, SuggestionChip.

API References: AssistChip ・ FilterChip ・ InputChip ・ SuggestionChip

docs.title: Badge
docs.text:
Small status indicator that decorates other widgets via a modifier. SmallBadge is a dot; LargeBadge shows a count.

API References: SmallBadge ・ LargeBadge

docs.title: Divider
docs.text:
Separator line, split by axis. HorizontalDivider draws a full-width line (sized with width); VerticalDivider draws a full-height line (sized with height). The cross-axis thickness comes from the style.

API References: HorizontalDivider ・ VerticalDivider

docs.title: Progress Indicators
docs.text:
Linear and circular progress, in determinate and indeterminate variants. LoadingIndicator is the M3 Expressive shape-morphing indicator.

API References: LinearProgressIndicator ・ CircularProgressIndicator ・ LoadingIndicator

docs.title: NavigationRail
docs.text:
Vertical navigation bar with collapsed / expanded states, badges, and an optional menu button. Pairs with Material Navigator for routing.

API Reference

docs.title: Toolbar
docs.text:
Action bar of icon buttons. DockedToolbar stretches to its container; HorizontalFloatingToolbar / VerticalFloatingToolbar are pill-shaped overlays laid out along their respective axis. Button / IconButton children are recommended per MD3; other widgets (including tooltip-wrapped buttons) are laid out as-is. A button without a style takes the toolbar's colour scheme; a button given a style keeps it. fab= places a Fab after the pill and colours it the same way.

API References: DockedToolbar ・ HorizontalFloatingToolbar ・ VerticalFloatingToolbar

docs.title: Menu
docs.text:
Vertical list of MenuItems. Supports leading icons, trailing shortcut/affordance text, dividers, and disabled items.

API Reference

docs.title: Tooltip
docs.text:
Contextual hint shown next to a target. Tooltip is a plain text label; RichTooltip supports a title, body, and action buttons.

API References: Tooltip ・ RichTooltip

docs.title: StandardSideSheet
docs.text:
Docked side panel that sits beside the main content area. Unlike the modal SideSheet, it is a permanent part of the layout. Pass a writable Observable[bool] as opened and the sheet animates its own width open and closed, staying mounted throughout.

opened: nv.Observable[bool] = nv.Observable(True)

nv.Row([
    main_content,
    nv.StandardSideSheet(panel_content, headline="Filters", opened=opened),
])

The close icon button writes opened.value = False by default. Pass on_close_click to intercept the press instead — the callback replaces the default, so updating opened becomes your responsibility:

def confirm_close() -> None:
    if vm.has_unsaved_changes:
        vm.show_confirm_dialog()
    else:
        opened.value = False

nv.StandardSideSheet(panel_content, opened=opened, on_close_click=confirm_close)

With a literal opened=True and no on_close_click, no close button is rendered: a press would have nothing to act on.

API Reference

docs.title: DockedDatePicker
docs.text:
A text field with a trailing calendar icon button. Tapping the icon opens a calendar in a dropdown anchored below the field; the date can also be typed directly.

value is the field's text, not a date. The date is derived from it, and so is anything the application wants to say about it — the widget flags nothing on its own, so is_error and supporting_text are derived from the same text and passed in.

self.arrival_text = nv.Observable("")
self.arrival = self.arrival_text.map(nv.parse_date)      # date | None

nv.DockedDatePicker(value=self.arrival_text, label="Arrival")

See Typed Values from Text Input for the recipe, and nv.DateFormat for a pattern other than mm/dd/yyyy.

The calendar renders English month names and weekday initials in a Sunday-first grid on every platform — it never reads the process locale. To localize it, pass nv.CalendarLabels:

import calendar

nv.DockedDatePicker(
    value=self.arrival_text,
    label="Anreise",
    date_format=nv.DateFormat("dd.mm.yyyy"),
    labels=nv.CalendarLabels(
        month_names=("Januar", "Februar", "März", "April", "Mai", "Juni", "Juli",
                     "August", "September", "Oktober", "November", "Dezember"),
        weekday_labels=("Mo", "Di", "Mi", "Do", "Fr", "Sa", "So"),  # Monday first
        first_day_of_week=calendar.MONDAY,
    ),
)

weekday_labels is always given Monday-first (indexed like date.weekday()), whatever first_day_of_week says; the default first day is Sunday, per MD3. The header always shows the month before the year, even for languages that write the year first. DatePicker, the inline calendar, takes the same labels.

API Reference

docs.title: Image
docs.text:
Image is a primitive widget that is not part of Material Design. Displays a raster image from in-memory bytes. Supports contain, cover, fill, and none fit modes.

API Reference

docs.title: Theme Extensions
docs.text:
Theme itself is design-agnostic — it is simply a container for a list of ThemeExtension objects. Built-in widgets such as Button and Checkbox depend on MaterialThemeData being registered in that list. You can attach your own extensions to the same list to inject additional design-system data without interfering with Material.

Import convention

ThemeExtension is available from the aggregate nuiitivet.material namespace:

import nuiitivet.material as nv

docs.title: Why extensions?
docs.text: Concern Mechanism Keep Theme design-agnostic Theme holds no built-in color roles. All data lives in extensions. Support multiple independent concerns Each extension has a distinct type; theme.extension(T) retrieves exactly one. Enforce uniqueness Registering two extensions of the same type raises ValueError.

docs.title: Retrieving an extension
docs.text:
import nuiitivet.material as nv

mat = nv.Theme.of(self).extension(MaterialThemeData)  # returns MaterialThemeData | None

Always guard the result against None — extension() returns None when the extension is not present or when the widget is not yet mounted.

docs.title: Use case 1 — Custom widget backed by a ThemeExtension
docs.text: This pattern is for authors building custom widgets that need app-specific colors or sizes that do not belong to Material.

docs.title: Step 1: Define the extension
docs.text:
from dataclasses import dataclass, replace

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class AppBrandTheme:
    brand_primary: str = "#1A6B3C"
    brand_on_primary: str = "#FFFFFF"
    brand_surface: str = "#E8F5E9"
    brand_accent: str = "#FF6F00"

    def copy_with(self, **kwargs) -> "AppBrandTheme":
        return replace(self, **kwargs)

@dataclass(frozen=True) satisfies the ThemeExtension protocol automatically — all that is required is a copy_with method.

docs.title: Step 2: Build a theme that includes both extensions
docs.text:
import nuiitivet.material as nv

def make_theme() -> nv.Theme:
    base = nv.ThemeFactory.light("#1A6B3C")
    return nv.Theme(
        mode=base.mode,
        extensions=[*base.extensions, AppBrandTheme()],
        name="app-brand-light",
    )

MaterialThemeData (from ThemeFactory) and AppBrandTheme coexist in the same extensions list. Each has a unique type, so there is no conflict.

docs.title: Step 3: Read the extension inside a widget
docs.text:
import nuiitivet.material as nv

class BrandCard(nv.ComposableWidget):
    def __init__(self, heading: str, content: str) -> None:
        super().__init__()
        self.heading = heading
        self.content = content

    def build(self) -> nv.Widget:
        brand = nv.Theme.of(self).extension(AppBrandTheme)
        bg     = brand.brand_surface if brand else "#E8F5E9"
        accent = brand.brand_accent  if brand else "#FF6F00"
        ...

docs.title: Full sample
docs.text: See the complete runnable example: samples/design-system/theme_extensions/custom_widget.py

docs.title: Use case 2 — Light / Dark support
docs.text: This use case extends BrandCard from Use case 1 to support runtime light / dark switching. Two AppBrandTheme variants — one for each mode — are swapped in by a toggle button.

docs.title: Step 1: Add required fields (no defaults)
docs.text:
Remove the default values so each theme factory is forced to supply explicit colors for its mode:

import nuiitivet.material as nv

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class AppBrandTheme:
    brand_surface: str     # no default — must be set per mode
    brand_on_surface: str  # text color on brand_surface
    brand_accent: str

    def copy_with(self, **kwargs) -> nv.ThemeExtension:
        return replace(self, **kwargs)

docs.title: Step 2: Create separate light and dark factories
docs.text:
import nuiitivet.material as nv

def make_light_theme() -> nv.Theme:
    base = nv.ThemeFactory.light("#1A6B3C")
    return nv.Theme(
        mode=base.mode,
        extensions=[*base.extensions, AppBrandTheme(
            brand_surface="#E8F5E9",
            brand_on_surface="#1B2A1F",
            brand_accent="#FF6F00",
        )],
        name="app-brand-light",
    )

def make_dark_theme() -> nv.Theme:
    base = nv.ThemeFactory.dark("#1A6B3C")
    return nv.Theme(
        mode=base.mode,
        extensions=[*base.extensions, AppBrandTheme(
            brand_surface="#1B3A2A",
            brand_on_surface="#C8E6C9",
            brand_accent="#FFB300",
        )],
        name="app-brand-dark",
    )

docs.title: Step 3: Change nothing in the widget
docs.text:
BrandCard already reacts to theme changes. It reads the extension inside build(), and that read is what makes it reactive:

import nuiitivet.material as nv

class BrandCard(nv.ComposableWidget):
    def __init__(self, heading: str, content: str) -> None:
        super().__init__()
        self.heading = heading
        self.content = content

    def build(self) -> nv.Widget:
        brand  = nv.Theme.of(self).extension(AppBrandTheme)
        bg     = brand.brand_surface     if brand else "#1B3A2A"
        fg     = brand.brand_on_surface  if brand else "#C8E6C9"
        accent = brand.brand_accent      if brand else "#FFB300"
        ...

Structurally this is the Use case 1 widget: a constructor and a build(), with no lifecycle hooks. It reads the brand_on_surface field added in Step 1, and its fallbacks are the dark ones because dark is this app's initial theme — that is the whole difference. Supporting light/dark cost the widget nothing.

Theme.of(self) does two things: it resolves the theme, and it records that the enclosing build scope depends on it. When the theme changes, the framework rebuilds every scope that read it, so build() re-runs with the new extension values on its own.

docs.title: Full sample
docs.text: See the complete runnable example: samples/design-system/theme_extensions/custom_color_token.py

docs.title: Coexisting extensions
docs.text:
Multiple extensions of different types can live in the same Theme. The only constraint is that each type appears at most once:

import nuiitivet.material as nv

base = nv.ThemeFactory.light("#6750A4")

theme = nv.Theme(
    mode=base.mode,
    extensions=[
        *base.extensions,   # includes MaterialThemeData
        AppBrandTheme(brand_surface="#E8F5E9", brand_on_surface="#1B2A1F", brand_accent="#FF6F00"),
    ],
    name="full-light",
)

Each widget retrieves exactly the extension it needs via theme.extension(T), and is unaware of the others.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: Scenario Pattern Custom widget needs brand colors Define a ThemeExtension, read via theme.extension(T) in build() Custom widget needs light/dark adaptive colors Define separate ThemeExtension values per mode; widget code is unchanged Multiple independent design concerns Register each as a separate extension type in the same Theme

docs.title: The intuitive grammar
docs.text: Nuiitivet keeps the parts of other frameworks that were already intuitive, so most of it reads like something you know. This page builds one small card, a few lines at a time.

docs.title: Lay out with a widget tree and parameters
docs.text:
import nuiitivet.material as nv

nv.Column(
    [
        nv.Text("Clicks"),
        nv.Button("Add one"),
    ],
    gap=12,
    padding=20,
)

A screen is a tree of widgets, as in Flutter. Spacing and sizes are parameters: padding, gap, size(width, height). Those parameters are all that decides the layout.

In Flutter, a padding and a width are widgets wrapped around the text, so the nesting grows with every decoration:

// Flutter — not Nuiitivet
Padding(
  padding: EdgeInsets.all(12),
  child: SizedBox(
    width: 200,
    child: Text("Clicks"),
  ),
)

Here they are parameters of the widget itself:

nv.Text("Clicks", padding=12, width=200)

A size is a number, "auto" (fit the content), or "wt" — a share of the space that is left, what WPF writes as *. The count below takes the leftover and pushes the button to the right edge:

nv.Row(
    [
        nv.Text("0 times", width="wt"),
        nv.Button("Add one"),
    ],
    gap=12,
    width=200,
    cross_alignment="center",
)

There is no margin. Spacing is padding and gap only — the habit CSS authors settle into, made the rule. And every pair is horizontal first, then vertical: padding=(16, 8) is 16 left and right, as alignment and translate are x before y.

Layout has the rest, including Grid: tracks sized as in WPF, cells placed by area name as in CSS.

docs.title: Add everything else with modifiers
docs.text:
What is not layout — a background, rounded corners, a tooltip, a click — is attached as a modifier. Modifiers chain with |, the way they chain in SwiftUI and Compose:

nv.Text("Clicks", padding=12, width=200).modifier(
    nv.background("#BBDEFB") | nv.corner_radius(8)
)

So the code itself tells the two apart: the parameters are the layout, the modifier chain is everything else. Modifiers lists them.

docs.title: Show state by binding it
docs.text:
count = nv.Observable(0)

nv.Text(count.map(lambda n: f"{n} times"))  # follows count on its own

Observable is modelled on ReactiveProperty, from WPF's MVVM. Hand the Observable to the widget and the widget follows it; there is no setState and nothing to refresh by hand. Observable covers deriving values and the Rx-style operators.

docs.title: Handle events with ordinary code
docs.text:
def handle_add(self) -> None:
    self.count.value += 1
    if self.count.value % 10 == 0:
        print("Milestone reached!")

nv.Button("Add one", on_click=self.handle_add)

What the screen shows is declared: the tree, and the values bound into it. What happens on a click is a different kind of thing — read a value, change it, branch on the result. That is a procedure. Forced into a declarative shape it only gets harder to follow, so a handler is an ordinary method, written top to bottom, the way you would say it aloud.

docs.title: The whole card
docs.text:
import nuiitivet.material as nv


class CounterCard(nv.ComposableWidget):
    def __init__(self) -> None:
        super().__init__()
        self.count = nv.Observable(0)

    def handle_add(self) -> None:
        self.count.value += 1
        if self.count.value % 10 == 0:
            print("Milestone reached!")

    def build(self) -> nv.Widget:
        return nv.Column(
            [
                nv.Text("Clicks", padding=12, width=200).modifier(nv.background("#BBDEFB") | nv.corner_radius(8)),
                nv.Row(
                    [
                        nv.Text(self.count.map(lambda n: f"{n} times"), width="wt"),
                        nv.Button("Add one", on_click=self.handle_add),
                    ],
                    gap=12,
                    width=200,
                    cross_alignment="center",
                ),
            ],
            gap=12,
            padding=20,
        )


def build_root() -> nv.Widget:
    return CounterCard()


nv.App(nv.Window(content=build_root)).run()
